questions.prompt: Do you prefer buying fresh food at a market or in a supermarket?

segments.text: I prefer buying fresh food at a market, although I have to admit I only go about once a month.
The fruit and vegetables are usually fresher, and you can chat to the seller and ask for advice about what's in season.
For instance, last summer I bought some peaches that tasted much better than anything I'd had from a supermarket.
That said, supermarkets are quicker and open later, so I still do my weekly shop there.
If I'm honest, it depends on what I'm after, but for fruit and vegetables I'd always choose a market.
What I like is that you can see exactly what you're getting, and the sellers tend to know where it's come from, which you rarely get with pre-packed produce.
A few weeks ago, a stallholder talked me out of buying melons that, in her words, weren't quite ripe yet, and she was right.
Supermarkets win on convenience, though, so I end up using both, depending on how much time I've got.

questions.prompt: Why do you think some people are willing to pay more for local food?

segments.text: I think there are a few reasons why people do that.
First, many believe local food tastes better because it hasn't travelled far, and it's often picked just a day or two before.
My aunt, for example, always buys eggs and cheese from a farm near her village, even though they cost more.
I'd guess people also like knowing that their money supports local farmers instead of big companies.
So for some people it's about quality, and for others it's about community.
I'd say it comes down to trust as much as taste.
When food is produced nearby, shoppers can ask questions, and that reassurance is worth a few extra pounds to many of them.
It's often the case that people who've visited a farm once become loyal customers for years.
There may also be an environmental angle, since shorter journeys must mean fewer emissions, although that isn't always as clear-cut as people assume.
Ultimately, I think what they're paying for is peace of mind.

It looks like a nice way to spend a day with the family.
The first thing that catches the eye is a family of four settled on a blanket in a park.

questions.prompt: How often do you eat outdoors?

segments.text: I eat outdoors fairly often, especially in spring and summer, probably once or twice a month.
Usually I go to a park or a beach with friends, and we bring sandwiches, fruit and something to drink.
Last month we had a barbecue by the river, and it was the best day I've had in ages.
I prefer eating outside because it's more relaxed than a restaurant, and it's cheaper too.
Not as often as I'd like, to be honest, but whenever the weather picks up I make a point of it.
There's something about eating in the open air that makes even a simple sandwich taste better, and it's a much easier way to catch up with people than meeting in a noisy restaurant.
Just last weekend, a few of us took a flask and some leftovers up to a hill near my town, and we stayed there until it got dark.
It's the company and the setting I enjoy, rather than the food itself.

questions.prompt: Do you think children spend enough time outdoors nowadays?

segments.text: No, I don't think they do, and I think it's a real problem.
Many children spend hours on tablets and games consoles, so they have less time to run around and play with friends.
When I was young, we played football in the street every afternoon, but now you hardly see any children out there.
I think parents might feel it's safer to keep them at home, and that's partly why things have changed.
Schools and families should encourage more outdoor activities.
I'd say not, although I'm wary of generalising.
Screens are obviously part of the picture, but I suspect parents are also far more cautious than they used to be, so children are rarely left to play unsupervised.
Where I grew up, we'd disappear for the whole afternoon, whereas nowadays most kids are collected from school and taken straight home.
That can't be good for their independence, and it might be one reason why so many children seem less active.
What we need is safer parks and more encouragement from schools.

questions.prompt: Would you prefer to work in an open-plan office or in a private office?

segments.text: I'd prefer to have a quiet space of my own, to be honest.
In an open-plan office it's difficult to concentrate because there are always phone calls and people talking nearby.
In my last job, I often stayed late just to finish my work in peace after everyone had left.
Having said that, open-plan offices make it easier to ask colleagues for help, so I can see the benefits.
It's a close call, but on balance I'd go for a private office.
I do my best work when I can think without interruption, and an open-plan layout makes that almost impossible, particularly for tasks that need sustained focus.
At my previous job, I'd often put on headphones just to get through a report, which rather defeats the point of sitting next to people.
That said, what I'd really want is a mixture: a quiet room for deep work and a shared space for team discussions.

questions.prompt: Why do you think more people work from home nowadays?

segments.text: I think there are two main reasons.
Firstly, technology has made it much easier, because video calls and online tools mean you don't need to be in the same room as your colleagues.
A friend of mine works for a company in London, but she lives in Spain and only goes to the office once or twice a year.
Secondly, I think companies have realised they can save money on office space, and employees might be happier too.
So in many cases it's good for both sides.
A number of factors have converged, in my view.
The pandemic proved that many jobs could be done remotely, and once employers saw that productivity hadn't collapsed, it was hard to go back.
Several people I know have turned down better-paid jobs simply because they'd have meant a long commute every day.
Companies may also have worked out that smaller offices mean lower rent, which can't be ignored in a tight economy.
It's a shift that suits both sides, though not every job allows it.

What we have here is a group of three friends sharing a table at a café, each with a coffee in front of them.

It's a scene many of us would recognise.

questions.prompt: How often do you meet your friends in cafés?

segments.text: I meet my friends in cafés about once a week, usually on Saturday mornings.
We normally go to the same place near the town centre because it's cheap and the coffee is good.
Last Saturday, we stayed there for almost three hours, just talking about our holidays and plans for the summer.
I enjoy it because it's a good way to relax and catch up after a busy week.
Pretty regularly, I'd say, roughly once a week, though it tends to slip when work gets busy.
We've got a favourite spot where the staff know our orders, and it's become something of a ritual, a chance to catch up properly instead of just swapping messages.
Last time, we ended up chatting for so long that the café was practically closing around us.
It's cheap, it's relaxing, and it's one of the highlights of my week.

questions.prompt: Do you think smartphones make it harder to enjoy time with friends?

segments.text: Yes, I think they can, but it depends on how people use them.
When everyone checks their phone every few minutes, it's difficult to have a proper conversation, and you can feel ignored.
Last week, I went out to dinner with a friend who kept answering messages, so I felt we weren't really spending time together.
I think a good idea is to put phones away during meals, and I try to do that myself.
On the whole, yes, though I'd hesitate to blame the phones themselves.
It's the constant pull of notifications that does the damage, because even if you don't look, you're half waiting for the next buzz, and that fractures your attention.
I've noticed that at dinners where we all leave our phones in a pile, conversations are noticeably livelier and last longer.
So the answer isn't to ban them, but to agree on some basic etiquette.

questions.prompt: Do you enjoy cooking, and what do you usually make?

segments.text: Yes, I do. I find cooking relaxing, especially after a long day at work.
I usually make simple dishes like pasta, omelettes or rice with vegetables because I don't have much time.
On Sundays I try something new, and last weekend I made a chicken curry for my family, which everyone loved.
I'd like to learn more recipes, because I think cooking is a really useful skill.
I do, more than I expected to, in fact; it's become my way of winding down.
During the week it's mostly quick, one-pan dishes, but at the weekend I like to take my time over something more ambitious.
Last Sunday I attempted a risotto from scratch, and although the rice was slightly overdone, my guests were kind enough to ask for seconds.
What I enjoy most is the creativity, since no two meals ever turn out exactly the same.

questions.prompt: Do you think people eat more healthily when they cook at home?

segments.text: Yes, generally I think they do.
When you cook at home, you know exactly what's in your food, and you can use fresh ingredients instead of a lot of salt, sugar or oil.
My brother started cooking his own meals last year, and he's lost weight and says he feels much more energetic.
However, it might not always be true, because some people just cook fried food or make huge portions.
So I think it depends on what you cook, but it's usually better than takeaways.
As a rule, yes, although it's not automatic.
Cooking at home gives you control over the ingredients and the portions, whereas ready meals and takeaways tend to be loaded with salt and fat.
A colleague of mine swapped her lunchtime sandwiches for home-made salads and, within a few months, she noticed a real difference in her energy levels.
Then again, anyone who fries everything in butter can hardly claim to be eating well, so it's less about where the food is made than what goes into it.
Still, cooking at home is where healthy habits tend to start.

questions.prompt: What was your favourite subject at school, and why?

segments.text: My favourite subject at school was English, which is probably why I'm learning it now.
I liked it because the teacher made the lessons fun, and we often did role-plays and watched short films.
Once we put on a short play in front of the whole school, and although I was nervous, it was a great experience.
It has also helped me a lot, because now I can read and talk to people from other countries.
History, without a doubt, though I wouldn't have predicted that when I started secondary school.
What won me over was a teacher who treated the past like a detective story, so instead of memorising dates, we had to work out why things had happened.
I remember we spent a whole week analysing a single letter from a soldier, and it was more gripping than most novels I'd read at that age.
Looking back, it's probably the subject that taught me to question what I read.

questions.prompt: How could schools make lessons more interesting?

segments.text: I think there are several things schools could do.
First, teachers could use more group work and projects, so students are active instead of just listening.
At my school, we once did a project about our town's history, and we interviewed older people. I learnt much more than from the textbook.
Technology might help as well, for example with videos or educational games.
In short, lessons should be more practical and less about copying from the board.
The key, I'd say, is to get students doing things rather than just receiving information.
Project-based learning works well because pupils have to apply what they've learned, and they're far more likely to remember something they've had to use.
A teacher I had once turned a lesson on percentages into a mock shop, and suddenly everybody was keen to get the sums right.
Technology could play a part too, though it ought to support the teaching, not replace it, otherwise it's just a gimmick.
Above all, a teacher's enthusiasm makes all the difference.
